meta.title: Who really said "I was a young man with uninformed ideas. I threw out queries, suggestions, wondering all the time over everything; and to my astonishment the ideas took like wildfire. People made a religion of them"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: No — Charles Darwin never said this. It is a line from the fabricated 1915 “Lady Hope” deathbed-conversion story, which Darwin’s own family denounced as false.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'I was a young man with uninformed ideas. I threw out queries, suggestions, wondering all the time over everything; and to my astonishment the ideas took like wildfire. People made a religion of them'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Darwin. It comes from the fabricated 1915 “Lady Hope” deathbed-conversion tale — invented words his children publicly denied.

answer.label: Not Charles Darwin — a fabricated deathbed quote
answer.sourceLine: These are not Darwin’s words. The line comes from the “Lady Hope story,” a fabricated account of Darwin’s supposed deathbed return to Christianity, first printed in the Boston Watchman-Examiner in August 1915 — 33 years after Darwin died. His children publicly denounced the whole story as false, and no such statement appears anywhere in Darwin’s letters or writings. Note that the popular wording “uninformed ideas” is itself a corruption of Lady Hope’s original “unformed ideas.”

source.heading: Where the line actually comes from
source.excerpt: I was a young man with unformed ideas. I threw out queries, suggestions, wondering all the time over everything; and to my astonishment the ideas took like wildfire. People made a religion of them.
trail: The Darwin Correspondence Project lists this exact line as one of the things Darwin never said, noting it “is in an article claiming to describe Darwin’s deathbed return to Christianity … generally considered to be a fabrication.”
Wikiquote files it under Misattributed, calling it “attributed to Darwin in another version of the Lady Hope fabrication.”
Wikipedia dates the original account to the Watchman-Examiner of 15 August 1915 (primary citations give 19 August 1915, p. 1071) and records the denials of Francis and Henrietta Darwin.
The TalkOrigins archive documents Henrietta Litchfield’s 1922 rebuttal in The Christian: “The whole story has no foundation whatever.”
source.excerptNote: As printed in Lady Hope’s 1915 narrative the phrase is “unformed ideas”; the widely circulated “uninformed ideas” is a later corruption. Either way, the words are Lady Hope’s invention, not Darwin’s.

source.rightsNote: The wording is not Darwin’s at all — it originates in Lady Hope’s article in the Boston Watchman-Examiner, first published 19 August 1915 (p. 1071). Because that source predates 1931 (and its author, Elizabeth Reid Cotton, died in 1922), the text is in the public domain in the United States. Public-domain status here reflects only the age of the printed source, not any endorsement that Darwin said it.

author.name: “Lady Hope” (Elizabeth Reid Cotton)
author.kicker: The real source of the words
author.heading: Who actually authored the line
author.bio: Elizabeth Reid Cotton became Lady Hope through her 1877 marriage to Admiral Sir James Hope. A prominent evangelist active in the temperance movement, she is remembered chiefly for the “Lady Hope story” — her 1915 claim to have visited a dying Charles Darwin and heard him lament his theory and turn to the Bible. The words she put in Darwin’s mouth, including this quote, are her invention; Darwin’s family flatly denied she was ever at his bedside.

misattribution.heading: A famous fabrication
misattribution.intro: This is one of the most durable fake quotes in the history of science — a fictional deathbed utterance manufactured to suggest Darwin abandoned his own theory.

items.why: Darwin never spoke or wrote these words. They appear only inside the “Lady Hope story,” a religious anecdote first printed in 1915, decades after his 1882 death. The Darwin Correspondence Project lists it among things Darwin never said.

Darwin’s daughter Henrietta Litchfield, who nursed him, declared in The Christian (1922) that Lady Hope “was not present during his last illness, or any illness” and that he “never recanted any of his scientific views,” per the TalkOrigins archive.
Lady Hope’s 1915 text reads “a young man with unformed ideas”; the popular internet version substitutes “uninformed ideas” — a later drift layered on top of an already-invented quote.

misattribution.truthLine: Bottom line: Charles Darwin never said this. It is invented dialogue from the fabricated 1915 Lady Hope deathbed story, which his family publicly and repeatedly denied.

context.heading: Why this quote exists
lead: The quote is one thread of the “Lady Hope story,” a piece of religious folklore that has circulated for over a century claiming Charles Darwin renounced evolution and embraced Christianity on his deathbed. It serves an obvious rhetorical purpose: if the author of On the Origin of Species himself recanted, so the argument runs, evolution must be doubtful.

In reality Darwin died on 19 April 1882 at Down House, nursed by his daughter Henrietta. Lady Hope’s account did not surface until August 1915, in an American Baptist newspaper, and every member of Darwin’s family who commented rejected it outright.
detailsBody: Francis Darwin (1917): “Lady Hope’s account of my father’s views on religion is quite untrue.”
Leonard Darwin later called the tale “purely fictitious” and a “hallucination.”
Henrietta Litchfield, in The Christian (23 February 1922): “Lady Hope was not present during his last illness, or any illness … The whole story has no foundation whatever.”
context.pull: “He never recanted any of his scientific views, either then or earlier.” — Henrietta Litchfield, 1922
